interviewQuestions.question: Why did tokenization move from whole words to subwords?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame this around two failures of word-level tokenization: it can't handle words outside a fixed vocabulary (rare words, typos, new terms all collapse to a single `<UNK>` token, losing information), and it scales poorly for morphologically rich languages where every inflection of a word becomes its own vocabulary entry. Subword schemes like BPE or WordPiece learn a vocabulary of frequent character chunks bottom-up from a training corpus, so common words stay intact as single tokens for efficiency, while rare or unseen words decompose into known pieces — "unhappiness" becomes "un" + "happi" + "ness" instead of `<UNK>`. That gives a fixed, bounded vocabulary size (typically 30k–50k tokens) with zero out-of-vocabulary failures — worst case it falls back to individual characters or bytes. That's why every modern Transformer (BERT, GPT, T5) uses a subword tokenizer rather than word-level splitting.

**Testing:** whether you understand the out-of-vocabulary problem and the vocabulary-size trade-off, not just that "subwords are used now".
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Word-level vs subword tokenization

interviewQuestions.question: Why can't a TF-IDF-based search or classifier tell 'the movie was not good' apart from 'the movie was good' in any meaningful way?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
TF-IDF is built on top of bag-of-words, and bag-of-words throws away word order entirely — a document is represented purely as counts (or weighted counts) of which words appeared, with zero information about the sequence they appeared in. "Not good" and "good" both contribute the token "good" to the vector with the same weight regardless of what preceded it; the word "not" just adds its own independent count in its own separate dimension of the vector, with no mechanism connecting it to the specific word it's negating. The model literally cannot represent the relationship "not" has to "good" in this sentence, because bag-of-words vectors have no concept of adjacency or relationship between dimensions at all — every word is an independent count in isolation.

Adding bigrams as a feature is the classical patch for exactly this problem: if "not good" is itself tracked as a single bigram feature distinct from the unigram "good," the vector can at least distinguish a sentence containing "not good" from one containing bare "good" as separate, non-overlapping signals. But this only handles the specific two-word combinations you explicitly track, and it still doesn't generalize — a bigram model would treat "not good" and "not great" as two completely unrelated features, with no notion that they're semantically similar negations, since there's still no shared representation connecting "good" and "great" at all.

The real fix is a fundamentally different representation — embeddings, and eventually attention-based contextual models — which can represent "not" as actually modifying the meaning of the word it precedes, because the representation is learned from co-occurrence patterns and context, not built from independent word counts.

**Testing:** whether you understand this as a structural limitation of bag-of-words (no order, no relationships between dimensions), not a fixable configuration issue.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why bag-of-words can't handle negation

interviewQuestions.question: You're building a search feature over product reviews and need to decide between TF-IDF, n-grams, and a Transformer embedding model. How would you reason through that choice given real constraints?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from what the search actually needs to match on, since that determines how much representational power is worth paying for. If most queries are close to literal keyword lookups — a specific product feature name, a brand, an exact phrase a reviewer might use — TF-IDF over unigrams (possibly with bigrams added) is a strong, cheap baseline: fast to compute, no training required beyond fitting on the corpus, easily explainable when debugging why a result matched, and computationally trivial at query time compared to running an embedding model per query. The known weakness — no notion of synonyms, no handling of negation, no semantic similarity across different phrasings — matters exactly to the extent that real user queries phrase things differently than reviews do.

I'd validate that assumption rather than guess: sample real or expected queries and check how often the "right" review uses different wording than the query ("battery dies fast" as a query should probably match a review saying "battery drains quickly" even with zero shared words) — if that mismatch is common, TF-IDF's blind spot to synonymy becomes a real product problem, not just a theoretical limitation, and that's specifically where embedding-based semantic search earns its cost: a Transformer embedding model captures that "dies fast" and "drains quickly" are semantically close even with no token overlap.

The practical middle ground I'd likely land on for a real product: start with TF-IDF/BM25 as a fast baseline to ship quickly and validate the feature's value, then add embedding-based retrieval in parallel (the same hybrid-retrieval pattern used in RAG and search ranking) once there's evidence the synonym-mismatch problem is costing real relevance — rather than reaching for the heaviest option by default before confirming it's actually needed.

**Testing:** whether you tie the representation choice to a concrete failure mode (synonym mismatch) you'd actually go measure, rather than defaulting to the most sophisticated option or the cheapest one on reflex.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Choosing a text representation for search, with real trade-offs
